youtube.baslik: Cochlear Implant Candidacy in Children and Adults | Lesson 236 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Who is a candidate for a cochlear implant? In this lesson we learn about limited benefit from hearing aids, candidacy criteria for adults and children, why early implantation matters, expanding criteria such as residual hearing and single-sided deafness, the reimbursement conditions of the Health Implementation Communiqué in Türkiye and the team decision.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Wolfe, Cochlear Implants: Audiologic Management and Considerations for Implantable Hearing Devices; Zwolan et al. (2020), Development of a 60/60 Guideline for Referring Adults for a Traditional Cochlear Implant Candidacy Evaluation, Otology and Neurotology; Sharma et al. (2002), A sensitive period for the development of the central auditory system in children with cochlear implants, Ear and Hearing; CMS, National Coverage Determination 50.3 Cochlear Implantation (2022); Social Security Institution, Health Implementation Communiqué (SUT), Türkiye, section 3.3.33.B Cochlear implant (current text at mevzuat.gov.tr).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn who is a candidate for a cochlear implant and how criteria for children and adults are set.
We will cover expanding criteria, the reimbursement conditions in Türkiye and why the decision is a team decision.

yan.metin: Not the threshold, but *benefit with hearing aids* decides

cumleler: Cochlear implant candidacy is decided not by a single threshold value but by looking at several findings together.
The key question is this: how much benefit does the person get from properly fitted hearing aids?
That is why limited benefit from hearing aids is the central concept of candidacy.
The cochlea and the auditory nerve must be suitable for an implant, and there must be no health problem that rules out surgery.
The realistic expectations of the person and family, and the support to keep up rehabilitation after surgery, are also assessed.
Criteria vary by country, device and reimbursement rules, and they have expanded markedly over the years.
In the early years, implants were given to adults who had no hearing left in either ear and whose language was already fully developed.
Then children became candidates, and the age of implantation kept falling.
As outcomes improved, people with severe loss who got partial benefit from hearing aids also began to be accepted as candidates.
For people with residual low-frequency hearing, hybrid approaches that preserve this hearing were developed.

cumleler.yazi: In the United States, some devices have also been approved for single-sided deafness since 2019.
cumleler.ses: In the United States, some devices have also been approved for single-sided deafness since twenty nineteen.

cumleler: This expansion means that many of today's candidates would not have been considered candidates a few decades ago.
In this example, a 68-year-old adult has a severe to profound loss in both ears that slopes toward the high frequencies.
The person has used hearing aids in both ears for years, and the aids are fitted to target with real ear measurement.
Even so, with the hearing aids, they score only 35 percent correct on a recorded open-set sentence test.
They cannot talk on the phone and cannot follow even family conversation without lipreading.
These findings show limited benefit despite properly fitted hearing aids, so the person is referred for an implant evaluation.
Age alone is not a barrier; older adults can also get meaningful benefit from an implant.
The values are examples; the actual decision is made after a full evaluation and a team discussion.

maddeler.metin: US public insurance: 60 percent or less

yan.metin: Better ear threshold *60 dB* or worse, unaided word recognition 60 percent or less: refer

cumleler: To speak of limited benefit, we must first show that the hearing aids are correctly fitted and verified with real ear measurement.
Then recorded open-set sentence and word tests are given in the best aided condition; live voice testing is not recommended.
Tests are done for each ear separately and for both ears together, and repeated in noise if needed.
Criteria vary with the manufacturers' approval documents; they usually describe moderate to profound loss and limited aided benefit.

cumleler.yazi: In 2022, US public insurance expanded its criterion to accept sentence recognition of 60 percent or less in the best aided condition.
cumleler.ses: In twenty twenty two, US public insurance expanded its criterion to accept sentence recognition of sixty percent or less in the best aided condition.

cumleler.yazi: The referral rule of Zwolan and colleagues: better ear average threshold of 60 dB or worse, unaided word recognition of 60 percent or less.
cumleler.ses: The referral rule of Zwolan and colleagues: better ear average threshold of sixty decibels or worse, unaided word recognition of sixty percent or less.

cumleler: This is a referral rule, not a candidacy decision; its aim is to get suitable people to evaluation in time.
One of the most important factors in adults is how long the severe loss has been present; the longer it lasts, the less the benefit may be.
Loss that begins after language develops, that is, postlingual loss, is usually linked to better open-set speech understanding.
People who have used hearing aids for years and kept up auditory input usually adapt to the implant faster.
The condition of the cochlear nerve and the cochlea can set limits on the benefit that can be achieved.
Family support, motivation and regular participation in rehabilitation also affect the outcome markedly.
These factors do not prevent candidacy, but they call for expectations tailored to each person.

yan.metin: The auditory brain is most plastic *in the early years*

cumleler: In children, the main criterion is bilateral severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss.
Because speech tests cannot be done in young children, benefit is judged by how auditory skills and language develop with hearing aids.
For this judgment to be meaningful, the child must wear hearing aids consistently and receive intervention.
If aided thresholds cannot make a large part of speech sounds audible, that is also a sign of limited benefit.

cumleler.yazi: In the United States, the approved lower age limit for some devices has been 9 months since 2020.
cumleler.ses: In the United States, the approved lower age limit for some devices has been nine months since twenty twenty.

cumleler: In children with congenital profound loss, early implantation is generally linked to better outcomes in language development.

cumleler.yazi: According to Sharma and colleagues, cortical responses approach normal in children implanted before about three and a half years of age.

cumleler: Newborn screening is completed by one month; we saw this earlier as the one, three, six goal.
Diagnosis is made by three months at the latest, and the degree of loss is found with electrophysiological tests.
Hearing aids are fitted without delay, and family-centered intervention starts before six months.
During the aided period, the child's auditory development is closely tracked; if progress is limited, an implant evaluation begins.
For a suitable child, the implant is planned as early as possible within the country's legal and reimbursement conditions.
A delay at any of these stages means losing part of the period when the auditory brain is most plastic.
In hearing loss after meningitis, the cochlea can ossify and make electrode insertion harder, so evaluation is done quickly.
If imaging shows that ossification has begun, the decision process may be brought forward even more.
In auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, the degree of loss reflects benefit poorly, so aids and rehabilitation are tried before deciding.
In inner ear malformations and cochlear nerve deficiency, the decision is shaped by imaging; we will see these in later lessons.
Children with additional disabilities can also be candidates, but goals and expectations are set individually with the family.
In progressive losses such as enlarged vestibular aqueduct, candidacy can change over time, so regular monitoring is needed.
In people with usable low-frequency hearing, electroacoustic stimulation can be used while preserving residual hearing.
In these people, low frequencies are stimulated acoustically and high frequencies electrically.
In single-sided deafness, implants are used in some countries to help with sound localization and understanding in noise.
Asymmetric losses, where one ear benefits from a hearing aid and the other does not, are assessed in a similar way.
Implants in both ears are used, especially in young children, to provide the advantages of hearing with two ears.
Older age alone is not a barrier; the decision depends on general health and the person's goals.
In this example, the right ear has a profound loss remaining after sudden hearing loss, and the left ear has normal hearing.
The person's main complaints are not knowing where sound comes from and not being able to follow speech in crowded places.
In this situation, systems that route sound to the better ear and bone conduction devices are also among the options.
An implant, by contrast, aims to restimulate the poorer ear itself; benefit has been reported for sound localization.
Which option is suitable depends on the person's goals, the duration of the loss and the country's approval and reimbursement rules.
In Türkiye, implant costs are covered under the Health Implementation Communiqué of the Social Security Institution.
For children over two and adults, the average threshold at 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz must be worse than 80 decibels in both ears.
Alternatively, thresholds of 70 decibels or worse in one ear and 90 decibels or worse in the other are required.
In patients who can do a speech discrimination test, the score must be below 30 percent.
In children aged two or under, a sensorineural loss of more than 90 dB HL in both ears is required.
A medical board report must state that at least three months of bilateral hearing aid use gave no benefit.
Implants in children under twelve months are not covered; because these conditions can change, always check the current regulation.

maddeler.metin: Language age gap or postlingual loss

yan.metin: Reimbursement conditions are not the same as *clinical candidacy*; check the current regulation

cumleler: The medical board report is issued by three ear, nose and throat specialists working at the same institution.
It is accompanied by an assessment from an audiologist at the same institution and one from a psychologist or speech and language therapist.
The gap between language age and chronological age must be under four years, or the loss must have begun after language developed.
In addition, inner ear development and the cochlear nerve must be shown with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging.
For losses after meningitis, the three-month hearing aid trial is not required.
In auditory neuropathy, at least six months of rehabilitation without benefit must be documented.

cumleler.yazi: Simultaneous or sequential bilateral implants are covered in situations listed in the regulation, such as children aged 12 to 48 months.
cumleler.ses: Simultaneous or sequential bilateral implants are covered in situations listed in the regulation, such as children aged twelve to forty eight months.

cumleler: The audiologist carries out hearing tests, the hearing aid trial and aided speech tests.
The ear, nose and throat surgeon assesses medical and surgical suitability.
The radiologist interprets imaging of the cochlea and the auditory nerve.
The speech and language therapist assesses the child's communication development and rehabilitation needs.
The psychologist assesses expectations, adjustment and the family's capacity to sustain the process.
The final decision is made together with the team, after all this information has been shared with the person and family.

sahneler.metin: Do not delay referring a person who gets too little benefit from hearing aids for an implant evaluation. The evaluation is not a commitment; it lets them learn their options.
cumleler: A tip from the field: do not delay referring someone who still struggles with speech despite hearing aids for an implant evaluation.
In many countries, only a small share of adults who could benefit from an implant are reported to receive one.
Explain that the evaluation is not a commitment to surgery but a chance to learn about their options.
Reporting the hearing aid fitting, aided speech scores and the person's complaints in your referral speeds up the process.

maddeler.metin: Key: limited benefit from hearing aids
Criteria expanded: residual hearing, one side
SUT is for payment; check updates

cumleler: What decides cochlear implant candidacy is limited benefit from properly fitted hearing aids.
In children, evaluation and implantation are done without delay, because of the early period when the auditory brain is plastic.
Criteria have expanded to include people with residual hearing, single-sided deafness and older adults.
In Türkiye, the Health Implementation Communiqué sets reimbursement conditions, but the decision is always a team decision.

sahneler.soru: Under SUT, which audiological condition applies to an implant in a child under two?
sahneler.aciklama: Aged two or under: _more than 90 dB HL in both ears_, sensorineural loss.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: under the Health Implementation Communiqué in Türkiye, which audiological condition applies to a child aged two or under?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: a sensorineural loss of more than 90 dB HL in both ears.
The conditions can be updated as the regulation changes; in practice, always check the current text.
